title: Complexe de De Rham à puissance divisée [conférence de 1976 à l’IHÉS] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
The page proves a standard lemma about divided powers (PD structures). Setting: A → B is a ring homomorphism u, compatible with ideals with divided powers (A, I, γ) and (B, J, δ), meaning u(I) ⊂ J. Suppose I is generated, as a PD ideal, by a family (x_i)_{i∈I}. Equivalently, I is generated as an ordinary ideal by the x_i^{(p)} for p ≥ 1. Claim: if u(x_i^{(p)}) = u(x_i)^{(p)} for all i and p, then u is a PD morphism, i.e. u(ξ^{(q)}) = u(ξ)^{(q)} for every ξ ∈ I and every q.

The proof sketched on the page runs as follows.
(1) Write ξ = Σ_ℓ ξ_ℓ, with each ξ_ℓ a term λ·x_{i_1}^{(p_1)}⋯x_{i_r}^{(p_r)}.
(2) Apply the sum formula (Σ ξ_ℓ)^{(q)} = Σ_{q_1+…+q_r=q} ξ_1^{(q_1)}⋯ξ_r^{(q_r)}, which holds on both sides. Since u is a ring map, this reduces the claim to individual terms: u(ξ_ℓ^{(q')}) = u(ξ_ℓ)^{(q')} for all q'.
(3) Scalars come out via (λx)^{(q)} = λ^q x^{(q)}.
(4) Products of monomials are handled by (ab)^{(q)} = a^q b^{(q)} for a ∈ I. This reduces everything to a single factor x^{(p)}.
(5) For that factor, use (x^{(p)})^{(q)} = c_{p,q} x^{(pq)} with c_{p,q} = (pq)!/((p!)^q q!). Then u((x^{(p)})^{(q)}) = c_{p,q} u(x)^{(pq)} = (u(x)^{(p)})^{(q)}.

The page carries this out twice. The upper half is in a functorial guise: u_* : Γ F(X) → F Γ(X), continuing the previous page on maps Γ^p F(X) → F Γ^p(X) and the compatibility u_{pq} with the composite Γ^q Γ^p → Γ^{pq}. The lower half is the concrete ring version.

The purpose is foundational groundwork for the 1976 IHÉS talk on the divided-power de Rham complex. The next page then axiomatizes PD structures on a pair (A, J → A) with J a non-unital algebra.
errors: The reduction leaves some steps implicit. One must use that u(I) ⊂ J. One must also use that the monomials x_{i_1}^{(p_1)}⋯x_{i_r}^{(p_r)}, with A-coefficients, span I. Only then do the sum and product formulas apply. These are standard and the argument is correct.
The overwritten line u(λ^q (x^{(p)})^{(q)}) = u(λ)^q (u(x_i)^{(p)})^{(q)} is correct. It silently uses the case p,q already established.

ideas.what: A ring map compatible with PD ideals is a PD morphism as soon as it commutes with the divided powers of a family of PD generators of the source ideal.
ideas.modern_name: Criterion for PD morphisms via generators
ideas.usually_credited_to: Berthelot (Cohomologie cristalline, LNM 407, 1974, Ch. I); Berthelot–Ogus, Notes on crystalline cohomology (1978), §3
ideas.where_published: Standard lemma in Berthelot 1974 and Berthelot–Ogus; also in the Stacks Project (divided power algebra chapter)

ideas.what: Use of the identities (x^{(p)})^{(q)} = (pq)!/((p!)^q q!)·x^{(pq)} and (ab)^{(q)} = a^q b^{(q)} to reduce PD compatibility to generators.
ideas.where_published: Roby, Lois polynomes et lois formelles; Berthelot LNM 407

ideas.what: Functorial formulation: natural maps Γ^p F(X) → F Γ^p(X) and their compatibility with Γ^q Γ^p → Γ^{pq}, i.e. functors commuting with divided-power functors.
ideas.modern_name: Polynomial functors / PD functors; compatibility of strict polynomial functors with Γ

missed.claim: The page shows a routine verification of the standard PD-generator lemma. It is set inside an attempt to phrase divided-power structures functorially, via natural maps Γ^p F → F Γ^p. This hints at an operadic or polynomial-functor viewpoint on PD structures, but nothing beyond the classical lemma is completed here.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is of minor historical interest as evidence of Grothendieck's functorial approach to PD structures around 1976. There is no new result.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine, well-known lemma (Berthelot 1974). Its functorial framing is only sketched.
transcription_corrections: The lines 'u(Σ ξ_i^{(q_i)} - ξ_r^{(q_r)}) = Σ u(ξ_i)^{(q_i)} - u(ξ_r)^{(q_r)}' should read u(Σ_{q_1+…+q_r=q} ξ_1^{(q_1)}⋯ξ_r^{(q_r)}) = Σ u(ξ_1)^{(q_1)}⋯u(ξ_r)^{(q_r)}. The dashes are product dots or ellipses, not minus signs, and the subscript is 1, not i.
'ξ_ℓ = x_1^{(p_1)} ⋯ x_r^{(p_r)}': the products are written with ellipses, not differences.
'(x_1^{(p_1)}⋯x_{r-1}^{(p_{r-1})})^q (x_r^{(p_r)})^{(q)}': the exponent q on the first factor is an ordinary power, matching (ab)^{(q)} = a^q b^{(q)}.
Under the brace, '(x^{(p)})^{(q)}' is marked as c_{p,q} x^{(pq)}. The subscript p on x is likely spurious.
'F(δ^p_x)(x)' is probably F(γ^p_x)(x), matching the previous page's notation.
The second diagram line is likely Ǎ → B̌ (or ℐ → 𝒥) with u^♭. The left-hand symbol is uncertain.
'OPS.' is probably 'OPS' (on peut supposer, 'we may assume') or 'DPS'. The line reads: we may suppose x = λ x_i^{(p)}.
